text: Can you recreate this fouries series time doman frequecny

Given: Square-wave amplitude A., Square-wave period T., Fundamental angular frequency \omega=2\pi/T., Centered odd square-wave symmetry., Odd-harmonic Fourier-series structure., Dark navy two-dimensional visualization with luminous orange, blue, cyan, and magenta curves.
Find: The reconstructed time-domain waveform and the corresponding amplitude of each odd harmonic in the frequency domain.

1. Define the periodic square wave
   x(t)=begin casesA,&0<t<T/2\\-A,&T/2<t<Tend cases, x(t+T)=x(t)
   Begin with a square wave of amplitude A and period T. Repeat this waveform across several periods in the upper time-domain panel. The periodicity assumption allows the signal to be represented using sinusoidal components whose frequencies are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

2. Identify the fundamental angular frequency
   ω=(2π)/(T)
   The fundamental angular frequency is determined by the period. In the animation, label the first spectral spike by omega and place higher harmonic spikes at integer multiples of this frequency.

3. Add the fundamental sinusoid
   x₁(t)=(4A)/(π)sin (ω t)
   Show the first sinusoidal component in a luminous orange or cyan curve. This component has frequency omega and provides the broad, smooth shape of the reconstructed signal. In the lower panel, display one vertical spike at omega with amplitude 4A/pi.

4. Add the third harmonic
   x₃(t)=(4A)/(π) (sin (ω t)+(sin (3ω t))/(3) )
   Introduce the third harmonic at frequency 3omega. Its amplitude is one third of the fundamental amplitude. Animate the new sinusoid and then show the pointwise sum becoming flatter near the plateaus and steeper near the transitions.

5. Add the fifth and seventh harmonics
   x₇(t)=(4A)/(π) (sin (ω t)+(sin (3ω t))/(3)+(sin (5ω t))/(5)+(sin (7ω t))/(7) )
   Add the fifth and seventh harmonics sequentially. Use distinct colors for the individual sinusoidal components, while using a brighter combined curve for their sum. The lower spectrum should now contain spikes at omega, 3omega, 5omega, and 7omega, with visibly decreasing heights.

6. Generalize to the finite odd-harmonic approximation
   SN(t)=(4A)/(π)∑ₘ=₀ᴺ(sin big ((2m+1)ω tbig ))/(2m+1)
   Replace the individually displayed terms by a finite sum containing the first N+1 odd harmonics. During the animation, increase N so that more harmonics are added. The upper curve approaches the square wave away from discontinuities, while small oscillatory overshoots remain near the jumps.

7. Connect each time-domain term to a frequency-domain spike
   frequency of term m=(2m+1)ω, amplitude of term m=(4A)/(π(2m+1))
   For every sinusoidal component in the upper panel, draw a corresponding vertical spike in the lower panel. The spike position records the harmonic frequency, and its height records the sinusoidal amplitude. Thus the time-domain sum and the frequency-domain spectrum describe the same signal in two complementary ways.

8. Show the limiting reconstruction
   x(t)=(4A)/(π) (sin (ω t)+(sin (3ω t))/(3)+(sin (5ω t))/(5)+·s )
   As more odd harmonics are included, the finite approximation approaches the square wave at points where the square wave is continuous. At a jump, the Fourier series converges to the midpoint of the two one-sided values, which is zero for this centered square wave. The animation should preserve the visible Gibbs overshoot near the discontinuities rather than implying perfect pointwise convergence there.

9. Final synchronized visual state
   x(t)=(4A)/(π) (sin (ω t)+(sin (3ω t))/(3)+(sin (5ω t))/(5)+·s )
   End with the reconstructed square wave in the upper panel and the complete odd-harmonic line spectrum in the lower panel. Label the horizontal axes as time and frequency, label the vertical quantities as amplitude, and annotate the transition from individual sinusoidal components to their summed waveform. The final mathematical expression is the same Fourier series used to generate the reconstructed curve.

Answer: x(t)=(4A)/(π) (sin (ω t)+(sin (3ω t))/(3)+(sin (5ω t))/(5)+·s )
A centered periodic square wave is reconstructed by adding its odd sinusoidal harmonics. The harmonic frequencies are \omega, 3\omega, 5\omega, and so on, while their amplitudes are proportional to 1, 1/3, 1/5, and so on. The upper panel shows the partial sums approaching the square wave, and the lower panel shows vertical spectral spikes at those odd harmonic frequencies with the corresponding decreasing amplitudes.

operations.title: Two views of one signal
operations.narration: A periodic signal can be viewed in time, as a waveform, or in frequency, as a collection of sinusoidal ingredients.

operations.title: The periodic square wave
operations.caption: x(t)=\begin{cases}A,&0<t<T/2\\-A,&T/2<t<T\end{cases},\qquad x(t+T)=x(t)
operations.narration: Start with a square wave of amplitude A. It stays high for half a period, low for half a period, and then repeats.

operations.title: Finding the fundamental
operations.caption: \omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
operations.narration: A period T corresponds to a fundamental angular frequency of two pi over T. This is the first location in the spectrum.

operations.title: The first harmonic
operations.caption: x_1(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\sin(\omega t)
operations.narration: The fundamental sinusoid gives the broad shape of the square wave. Its frequency is omega, and its spectral amplitude is 4A over pi.

operations.title: Adding the third harmonic
operations.caption: x_3(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}\right)
operations.narration: Now add a sinusoid three times as fast, but only one third as strong. Their sum begins to look much more like a square wave.

operations.title: More odd harmonics
operations.caption: x_7(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}+\frac{\sin(5\omega t)}{5}+\frac{\sin(7\omega t)}{7}\right)
operations.narration: The fifth and seventh harmonics sharpen the transitions further. Each new harmonic is faster and weaker than the previous one.

operations.title: The finite approximation
operations.caption: S_N(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\sum_{m=0}^{N}\frac{\sin\big((2m+1)\omega t\big)}{2m+1}
operations.narration: All of these partial sums follow one rule: include the first N plus one odd harmonics, each divided by its odd harmonic number.

operations.title: A term becomes a spike
operations.caption: \text{frequency of term }m=(2m+1)\omega,\qquad \text{amplitude of term }m=\frac{4A}{\pi(2m+1)}
operations.narration: Every sinusoid leaves one spike in the spectrum. The spike position records its frequency, and its height records its amplitude.

operations.title: The limiting reconstruction
operations.caption: x(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}+\frac{\sin(5\omega t)}{5}+\cdots\right)
operations.narration: As more odd harmonics are added, the partial sum approaches the square wave wherever the wave is continuous. At a jump, it converges to zero, while the Gibbs overshoot remains visible nearby.

operations.title: FINAL ANSWER
operations.caption: x(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}+\frac{\sin(5\omega t)}{5}+\cdots\right)
operations.narration: The centered square wave is reconstructed by adding its odd sinusoidal harmonics. The frequencies are omega, 3 omega, 5 omega, and so on, and their amplitudes decrease in proportion to 1, one third, one fifth, and so on.
